content: Antibiotics offer only a modest benefit in treating sore throat, but their effectiveness increases in individuals with confirmed group A beta-haemolytic streptococci (GABHS) infections. However, it remains unclear which antibiotic is the optimal choice when treatment is indicated. This review, updated from previous versions published in 2010, 2013, 2016, and 2021, aimed to evaluate the comparative efficacy of different antibiotics in alleviating symptoms such as pain and fever, shortening the duration of illness, preventing clinical relapse (recurrence of symptoms after initial resolution), and preventing complications such as suppurative complications, acute rheumatic fever, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Additionally, the review assessed the incidence of adverse effects and the risk-benefit profile of antibiotic treatment for streptococcal pharyngitis. The review included randomized, double-blind trials that compared different antibiotics and reported outcomes such as clinical cure, clinical relapse, complications, and/or adverse events. A total of 19 trials, reported in 18 publications, were included, involving 5839 randomized participants. These trials compared various antibiotics, including penicillin, cephalosporins, macrolides, carbacephem, sulphonamides, clindamycin, azithromycin, and amoxicillin. Participants ranged in age from one month to 80 years, with nine trials focusing predominantly on children. Most studies were conducted in outpatient settings, and all participants had confirmed acute GABHS tonsillopharyngitis. The quality of the included studies was generally poor, with inadequate reporting of randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding. The certainty of the evidence was downgraded due to these methodological limitations, as well as heterogeneity and wide confidence intervals. Cephalosporins versus Penicillin: The evidence is uncertain regarding whether cephalosporins are more effective than penicillin in resolving symptoms within 2 to 15 days (odds ratio [OR] for absence of symptom resolution: 0.79, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.55 to 1.12; 5 trials, 2018 participants; low-certainty evidence). Sensitivity analysis of evaluable participants suggested a potential benefit for cephalosporins (OR: 0.51, 95% CI: 0.27 to 0.97; 5 trials, 1660 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Clinical relapse may be lower with cephalosporins compared to penicillin (OR: 0.55, 95% CI: 0.30 to 0.99; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome [NNTB]: 50; 4 trials, 1386 participants; low-certainty evidence). There was no significant difference in reported adverse events (very low-certainty evidence). Macrolides versus Penicillin: The evidence is uncertain regarding differences in symptom resolution between macrolides and penicillin (OR: 1.11, 95% CI: 0.92 to 1.35; 6 trials, 1728 participants; low-certainty evidence). Sensitivity analysis of evaluable participants yielded an OR of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.57 to 1.09; 6 trials, 1159 participants). Clinical relapse rates were also uncertain (OR: 1.21, 95% CI: 0.48 to 3.03; 6 trials, 802 participants; low-certainty evidence). Children treated with macrolides appeared to experience more adverse events compared to those treated with penicillin (OR: 2.33, 95% CI: 1.06 to 5.15; 1 trial, 489 participants; low-certainty evidence). However, subgroup differences between children and adults were not statistically significant. Azithromycin versus Amoxicillin: Based on one unpublished trial in children, the evidence is uncertain regarding whether azithromycin in a single dose is more effective than amoxicillin administered for 10 days in resolving symptoms (OR: 0.76, 95% CI: 0.55 to 1.05; 1 trial, 673 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Sensitivity analysis for per-protocol analysis suggested a potential benefit for azithromycin (OR: 0.29, 95% CI: 0.11 to 0.73; 1 trial, 482 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Relapse rates were also uncertain (OR: 0.88, 95% CI: 0.43 to 1.82; 1 trial, 422 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Adverse events were more common with azithromycin compared to amoxicillin (OR: 2.67, 95% CI: 1.78 to 3.99; 1 trial, 673 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Carbacephem versus Penicillin: Low-certainty evidence suggests that carbacephem may provide better symptom resolution compared to penicillin in adults and children (OR: 0.70, 95% CI: 0.49 to 0.99; NNTB: 14.3; 3 trials, 795 participants). However, long-term complications were not reported, making it unclear whether carbacephem is superior in preventing serious but rare complications. Conclusions: The evidence does not demonstrate clinically relevant differences in symptom resolution when comparing cephalosporins and macrolides with penicillin for the treatment of GABHS tonsillopharyngitis. Low-certainty evidence suggests that carbacephem may be more effective than penicillin for symptom resolution in children. There is insufficient evidence to draw conclusions regarding other antibiotic comparisons. Data on complications were too limited to make definitive conclusions. Overall, antibiotics have a limited effect in treating GABHS pharyngitis, and the findings do not indicate that other antibiotics are more effective than penicillin. In the context of antimicrobial stewardship, penicillin remains a suitable choice when antibiotic treatment is indicated. All included studies were conducted in high-income countries with a low risk of streptococcal complications, highlighting the need for trials in low-income countries and disadvantaged populations where the risk of complications is higher.
